Paper [5] explicitly addresses the privacy of the last iterate in DP-SGD under nonconvex composite losses, aiming to minimize noise while maintaining privacy guarantees. Paper [9] also focuses on privacy analysis for DP-SGD in the hidden state setting, where only the final model is released, and provides tighter bounds compared to standard composition analysis. Paper [11] also proposes tighter privacy auditing for DP-SGD under the hidden state threat model, using numerical methods to challenge the gap between empirical auditing and theoretical upper bounds. Both papers employ substantively equivalent mechanisms for deriving tighter privacy guarantees under similar assumptions. Therefore, the mechanism is covered.

Paper [9] evaluates its privacy analysis by comparing theoretical bounds against empirical auditing results, which is substantively equivalent to comparing against standard composition analysis. Paper [5] also evaluates its privacy accounting by deriving theoretical bounds and comparing them to existing methods. Both papers use the same evaluation design: theoretical derivation of privacy bounds and comparison against standard methods. Therefore, the evaluation is covered.

### Domain Reasoning:
The contribution operates in the domain of differential privacy, specifically DP-SGD privacy analysis. Papers [5], [9], and [11] all work in the same general application area of DP-SGD privacy analysis, even though they target specific sub-problems or settings (e.g., hidden state, last iterate). The domain is therefore covered.

## Purpose

The contribution's purpose is: give tighter privacy loss estimates than standard composition analysis when only the **last iterate** of DP-SGD is released (hidden state / last-iterate setting).

- Paper [5]: "Tight DP accounting for the last iterate would minimize the amount of noise required while maintaining the same privacy guarantees" — directly addresses last-iterate privacy in DP-SGD.
- Paper [9]: "the privacy analysis of DP-SGD makes the unrealistic assumption that all intermediate iterates are released... only the final trained model... is released. In this hidden state setting, prior work has provided tighter..." — same purpose.
- Paper [10]: "When the internal state of the algorithm is hidden, we prove a converging privacy bound" — same purpose of tighter bounds in hidden-state setting.
- Paper [11]: "we focus on a threat model where the adversary has access only to the final model... a significant gap between the lower bound from empirical privacy auditing and the theoretical upper bound" — same purpose.
- Paper [15]: "The hidden state threat model of differential privacy (DP) assumes that the adversary has access only to the final trained machine learning (ML) model" — same purpose.

Papers [5], [9], [10], [11], [15] all share the same purpose.

## Mechanism

The contribution's mechanism: assume linear loss (enabling exact analysis), derive (ε,δ)-DP guarantees for the last iterate via hockey-stick divergence (computable with existing DP accounting libraries), then extrapolate heuristically to nonlinear deep learning losses.

- Paper [5]: "Privacy of the last iterate in cyclically-sampled DP-SGD on nonconvex composite losses" — analyzes last iterate privacy, but focuses on nonconvex composite losses with cyclic sampling, not a linear-loss heuristic extrapolation.
- Paper [9]: Focuses on showing no privacy amplification for hidden state DP-SGD with non-convex loss — different mechanism (impossibility result).
- Paper [10]: Uses contraction properties for strongly convex losses — not linear loss assumption + hockey-stick divergence heuristic.
- Paper [15]: "Convex Approximation of Two-Layer ReLU Networks" — uses convex approximation of neural networks, not linear loss assumption as worst-case proxy.
- Paper [13]: "Privacy Amplification by Iteration" — uses contractive iterations, not linear loss heuristic.
- Papers [3], [22]: PLD-based accounting and saddle-point accountant — these are DP accounting tools (hockey-stick divergence based), but don't specifically address the linear-loss-as-proxy heuristic for last iterate.

The specific mechanism — assuming linear loss as a tractable proxy/worst-case, deriving exact (ε,δ) guarantees via hockey-stick divergence for the last iterate, then extrapolating heuristically — does not appear to be covered by any prior paper. Paper [15] is closest (convex approximation for hidden state DP), but uses a different primitive (convex approximation of ReLU networks, not linear loss as worst-case).

## Evaluation

The contribution's evaluation: Theorem 1 gives exact closed-form; comparison against standard composition (Fig. 1); linear loss argued as worst-case for full-batch non-subsampled setting (Appendix B).

- Paper [11]: Compares privacy bounds against standard composition analysis and empirical auditing — same design of comparing tighter bounds vs. standard composition.
- Paper [5]: Similarly compares last-iterate privacy bounds against composition-based analysis.
- Paper [9]: Compares hidden-state bounds against composition bounds.
- Paper [10]: Proves converging bounds and compares against composition-based linear growth.

The evaluation design (comparing a proposed tighter bound against standard composition analysis) is covered by [9], [10], [11].

The contribution operates in differential privacy / DP-SGD privacy analysis. This is clearly covered by numerous papers: [1], [3], [4], [5], [7], [8], [9], [10], [11], [13], [14], [15], [16], [17], [22], etc.

While the specific datasets and models are new, the evaluation design itself — using membership inference/auditing attacks to compare empirical and theoretical privacy bounds — is covered by prior work. For example, [3], [6], and [23] all use similar evaluation designs to empirically audit privacy leakage in differentially private machine learning. The specific datasets and models used in this contribution are instances of a known evaluation design, not a new design logic. Thus, the evaluation facet is covered.

### Domain
The domain is privacy auditing in machine learning, specifically applied to vision (CIFAR-10) and language (Gemma 2) tasks. Privacy auditing is a well-established domain, as evidenced by numerous prior papers, including [1], [3], [6], [7], [18], and [23].
